faqs.question: Which Diwali story should I tell a three-year-old?
faqs.answer: Pick one with counting and repetition and no villain, like the 120-word "Where Did the Moon Go?" script above. At two to four, giving the child a job, such as shouting the word "light", holds attention better than a plot does.

faqs.question: How long should a Diwali story for kids be?
faqs.answer: Roughly 120 words for ages 2–4, 210 for ages 5–7 and 245 for ages 8–10, which is one to two minutes at about 110 words a minute (our estimate). Three questions bring each telling to three to five minutes.

faqs.question: Is the Ravana part too scary for young kids?
faqs.answer: It can be, so keep it to one sentence: Ravana "carried Sita off" and later "the battle was won". Under-fours do not need Ravana at all, and Sita's exile, which follows the homecoming in the full epic, is better saved for children of 11 and up.

faqs.question: What should I ask my child after telling the Diwali story?
faqs.answer: Mix the five CROWD types from dialogic reading: a completion prompt ("One diya, one ___"), a recall question, an open-ended one, a wh-question and a distancing question that links the story to their own life. One question per scene is enough.

faqs.question: Why do Tamil families take an oil bath before sunrise on Deepavali?
faqs.answer: Because much of South India celebrates Krishna and Satyabhama defeating Narakasura on Naraka Chaturdashi morning, which in 2027 falls on Thursday 28 October. Tamil Nadu holiday lists show 29 October while panchangs put Tamil Deepavali on the 28th, so check your local calendar.

faqs.question: When is Diwali in 2027?
faqs.answer: Lakshmi Puja, the main Diwali night, is Friday 29 October 2027. Dhanteras is Wednesday 27 October, Naraka Chaturdashi Thursday 28, Govardhan Puja Saturday 30 and Bhai Dooj Sunday 31 October.

faqs.question: How do I explain Diwali to a class with Jain and Sikh children?
faqs.answer: Tell it as several stories that share one night: Rama's homecoming, Krishna's rescue, Mahavira remembered by Jains and Bandi Chhor Divas for Sikhs. The 8–10 script does this through two cousins and their Nani, and asks children which stories end with someone coming home or set free.

faqs.question: Is a cartoon video as good as reading the Diwali story aloud?
faqs.answer: A video cannot wait for a child's answer, and the questions are the part research supports. A 2024 study of 111 children aged 3–7 found that discussion prompts eased comprehension gaps for inattentive children, so if you use a video, pause it and ask.

faqs.question: Can a grandparent abroad tell the Diwali story on a video call?
faqs.answer: Yes, and a live call beats a recording because the child can answer back. Afterwards, a SubhSandesh Diwali card in family mode gives the child a row of wish diyas to light and lanterns with up to six photos, though it is a greeting, not a storybook.

faqs.question: Can my child keep a Diwali card made after the story?
faqs.answer: On the SubhSandesh Diwali page, the Shubh Deepavali card at the end can be saved as a 1080×1920 image, and the link keeps working for later evenings. For a story you want read every year, a printed book is still the better keepsake.

faqs.question: Is the Diwali story the same as the Dussehra story?
faqs.answer: Both come from the Ramayana, but they mark different moments. Dussehra celebrates Rama's victory over Ravana, while the North Indian Diwali story is his homecoming to Ayodhya a few weeks later, which is why the scripts above end with lamps, not the battle.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Diwali Story for Kids: Read-Aloud Scripts by Age, With Questions

A good Diwali story for kids is short enough to finish before attention runs out and open enough for the child to talk back. Below are three original read-aloud scripts for ages 2–4, 5–7 and 8–10, each running three to five minutes once you add the questions that shared-reading research says turn listening into conversation.

Many of you will read from a screen: 48.4% of views of SubhSandesh pages happen on a phone or tablet. Plan for repeats: a SubhSandesh page is viewed 11.1 times on average, and a short script survives the tenth telling. Below are the scripts, the research, what to skip and how a faraway grandparent joins in.

## What is the Diwali story, told for a child?

The Diwali story is not one story but a handful of homecomings and rescues that families attach to the same moonless night, which in 2027 is Friday 29 October. For a child, the shortest honest version is: on a night with no moon, people light lamps to welcome back something good.

North Indian families mostly tell of Rama coming home to Ayodhya. Much of South India starts a morning early, on Naraka Chaturdashi (Thursday 28 October 2027; Tamil Nadu holiday lists say the 29th, panchangs the 28th), with Krishna and Satyabhama defeating Narakasura. Jains remember Mahavira; Sikhs mark Bandi Chhor Divas.

## Three Diwali read-aloud scripts, timed by age

Each script has four parts: who it suits, its length, the script and the questions. Timings assume about 110 words a minute, our estimate, not a measurement.

### 1. Ages 2–4: "Where Did the Moon Go?" (about 120 words)

**Who it suits:** toddlers who love counting and repeating; there is no villain.

> It is Diwali night. The sky is dark, dark, dark.
> "Where did the moon go?" asks Meera.
> "The moon is resting tonight," says Dadi. "So we make our own light."
> Dadi lights one clay diya. Meera keeps her hands in her lap and watches.
> "One diya," says Meera. "One light."
> Papa lights another. "Two diyas. Two lights."
> Baby Kabir claps. Mumma lights one more. "Three diyas! Three lights!"
> "Long ago," says Dadi, "a kind prince named Rama came home after a very long trip, and everyone lit lamps so he could find his way."
> "Like ours?" asks Meera. "Just like ours."
> Now the window glows. The door glows. The whole street glows. The sky is still dark, but Meera's home is bright, bright, bright.

**Ask:**

- Completion: "One diya, one ___." Let the child shout the last word.
- Wh-question: "Who lit the very first diya?"
- Distancing: "How many diyas can we count in our house tonight?"

### 2. Ages 5–7: "The Long Way Home" (about 210 words)

**Who it suits:** children who can hold a problem and a happy ending; each scary part is one sentence.

> Once there was a prince called Rama, and everybody in Ayodhya loved him. But his father, the king, had to keep an old promise, and it meant Rama must live in the forest for fourteen years. That is longer than you have been alive!
> Rama did not sulk. His wife Sita and brother Lakshmana went with him, because they would not let him go alone.
> One day Ravana, the proud king of Lanka, carried Sita off to his island across the sea. Rama was very sad, but he did not give up.
> A clever monkey named Hanuman leapt across the sea and whispered to Sita, "Rama is coming." Monkeys and bears built a bridge of stones over the water, the battle was won, and Sita was safe.
> They flew home in a magic chariot called the Pushpak. In Ayodhya, Rama's brother Bharata had looked after the kingdom the whole time. When he saw the chariot, he ran out with the biggest smile in the city.
> And the way families have told it ever since, when night fell, a night with no moon, people put little clay lamps on every doorstep so Rama could see his way home.
> That is why we light diyas. Each little flame says: welcome home.

**Ask:**

- Recall: "Why did Rama have to live in the forest?"
- Open-ended: "Tell me what Ayodhya looked like when Rama came back."
- Distancing: "Who would you light a lamp for, to welcome them home?"

### 3. Ages 8–10: "Two Mornings, One Light" (about 245 words)

**Who it suits:** children old enough to compare two versions and take a side.

> Arjun lived in Lucknow and his cousin Kavya in Chennai, and every Diwali they argued on a video call about whose Diwali came first.
> "Ours starts before sunrise," said Kavya, holding up a steel bowl of oil. "Paati wakes us at four. Oil bath, new clothes, sweets, all before it is light. Because of Narakasura. He was a king so greedy he took what belonged to everyone, even people, whom he locked in his fortress. Krishna went to stop him, and Satyabhama, Krishna's wife, drove the chariot. In lots of tellings she finishes the fight. The prisoners walked free, and people lit lamps before dawn."
> "Ours is about Rama coming home to Ayodhya," said Arjun. "Yours is a homecoming," said Kavya, "and mine is a jailbreak."
> "A rescue. Jailbreak makes Krishna sound like the bad guy."
> They laughed so hard the call froze. When it came back, Nani was leaning into the screen. "You are both right. My friend Mrs Shah is Jain, and tonight she remembers Lord Mahavira, whose followers lit lamps so his teaching would keep shining. The Sikh family next door celebrates Bandi Chhor Divas, when Guru Hargobind left prison only after the other prisoners were freed too. Count how many stories end with someone coming home or set free."
> Kavya counted. "All of them."
> "Now set out the diyas," said Nani. "Carefully, and not near the curtains."
> "See you at four," said Kavya. "Not a chance," said Arjun. But he set an alarm anyway.

**Ask:**

- Recall: "What did Narakasura take that was not his?"
- Open-ended: "Kavya says jailbreak and Arjun says rescue. Who is right, and why does the word matter?"
- Distancing: "What story does our family tell on Diwali, and who told it to you first?"

## Why the questions matter: PEER and CROWD in two minutes

The questions come from dialogic reading, in which the adult asks and the child does most of the telling. [Dicataldo and colleagues' 2022 study of 40 Italian preschoolers](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC9406408) sets out its memory aids: PEER (prompt, evaluate, expand, repeat) for how the adult responds, and CROWD (completion, recall, open-ended, wh- and distancing questions) for what to ask. Their six-week parent programme produced sustained language gains.

In a [2026 PLOS ONE study by Sia and colleagues](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13268133), parents of 2-year-olds were filmed during a five-minute picture-book session; the more dialogic the parent, the stronger the child's frontal-brain activation in a rule-switching task at age 5. That is a correlation in 53 recruited children, not proof that one story changes a brain.

[Yang and colleagues (2024)](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC11579648) found, with 111 children aged 3–7, that discussion prompts in a story e-book eased the comprehension gap for children showing inattention or hyperactivity. Ask one question per scene, and repeat each answer with one more word: "Lamp!" becomes "A clay lamp, yes."

## The three Diwali scripts side by side

| Script | Age band | Script words | Reading time at ~110 words a minute (EST) | Questions | Left out on purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| "Where Did the Moon Go?" | 2–4 | 120 | about 1 minute | 3 | Any villain or conflict |
| "The Long Way Home" | 5–7 | 210 | about 2 minutes | 3 | How Sita was taken, how the battle went |
| "Two Mornings, One Light" | 8–10 | 245 | about 2 minutes | 3 | Sita's later exile, how Naraka died |

The questions add two or three minutes to each script. If time runs short, cut the script, not the questions.

## Which Diwali story scenes to leave out for under-8s

The full Ramayana carries an abduction, a war, a fire ordeal and Sita's exile. John Campbell Oman's 1900 retelling, [The Great Indian Epics on Project Gutenberg](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/73417), shows how close those turns sit to the happy ending: it covers the Pushpak flight and Bharata's welcome in three sentences, then moves almost at once to the people mocking Rama and Sita being left alone in the forest.

So the scripts stop at the welcome. Ages 2–4 get no villain; ages 5–7 hear that Sita was "carried off" and "the battle was won"; ages 8–10 get a greedy king defeated. Save Sita's exile for 11 and up, when a child can argue about whether it was fair.

## Telling the story to a grandchild in another city

A video call beats a recording, because questions need a live answer. The grandparent reads; the child shouts the repeated lines.

The [interactive Diwali card on SubhSandesh](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-diwali) is not a storybook and reads nothing aloud, but its family mode fits the ending of every script: the child lights a row of diyas, each lifting one of your wishes, colours a rangoli until the initials glow, and lights sky lanterns holding up to six family photos. The crackers are drawn, with no noise or smoke. Put a 50-word "Where Did the Moon Go?" in the letter inside the shagun liffafa.

Build it a day early. With no Diwali data yet, here is Raksha Bandhan 2026 data used as the nearest festival analogue (n = 89): 49.4% of pages were built on the festival day itself and 27.0% the day before. For a child of six or more, the [photo jigsaw that reveals a letter piece by piece](https://subhsandesh.in/photo-puzzle) suits a family photo, though it is not a Diwali template.

## When a screen is the wrong place for a Diwali story

For children under two, skip the screen: the Sia study filmed parents with a printed picture book. At bedtime, say the 120-word script from memory.

A link also fails a child who cannot read yet and has no adult beside them, because the wishes and letter are text. And a book on the shelf has no link to lose. SubhSandesh is for the wish after the story, not the story.

## Sources

- Dicataldo et al., *Children*, 30 July 2022.
- Sia et al., *PLOS ONE*, 15 June 2026.
- Yang et al., *Child Development*, 18 June 2024.
- Oman, *The Great Indian Epics*, 1900 (public domain).
